title: Regular Long Runs and Higher Training Volumes Are Associated with Better Running Economy Durability in Performance Matched Well-Trained Male Runners
authors: Zanini M, Folland JP, Blagrove RC
population: Well-trained male runners matched on 10 km time (39:10 vs 39:00): 13 with regular long runs of 90 min or more vs 13 with all runs under 70 min
findings: During a 90-min run at lactate threshold, running economy worsened earlier and more in the short-run group: +6.0% vs +3.1% at 90 min (P<0.001).
Isometric squat force fell 19.4% vs 12.2% (P=0.002) and countermovement jump mean power changed -6.6% vs +2.2% (P=0.011), short vs long group.
The neuromuscular changes were not correlated with RE durability, whereas RE durability correlated with weekly longest run (r=-0.67, P<0.001) and training volume (r=-0.48, P=0.038).
Authors state intervention studies are needed to confirm these cross-sectional findings.
limitations: Cross-sectional, men only, 13 per group; association not causation (self-selection of runners who do long runs). Online 2025-08-29, print MSSE 2026 Jan;58(1):162-173; the print year 2026 is recorded, consistent with the other entries.
implications: Include a long run of at least 90 min as a weekly or fortnightly staple for athletes targeting half marathon and longer; supported by association only.
Use longest-run duration and weekly volume as covariates when predicting how much economy and pace will decay late in a race.

verification.notes: Year corrected from 2025 to 2026 to match print issue (PubMed 2026 Jan 1); id retains 2026. Numbers match PubMed abstract.
